summary: The RADIUS protocol is limited to a total packet size of 4096 bytes. Provisions exist for fragmenting large authentication data using Access-Challenge packets, but not for other kinds of data. This experimental document defines a way to fragment larger amounts of data across multiple packets.

eli5.summary: RADIUS messages have a size limit. This experiment says how to chop a big message into smaller pieces and put it together on the other side.

questions: why is radius packet size limited to 4096 bytes
subtitle: A way to send large amounts of authorization data by splitting RADIUS packets across multiple exchanges.

tldr.problem: The RADIUS protocol limits packets to 4096 bytes, and authentication servers and clients need to exchange large amounts of authorization data (such as SAML statements) that exceed this limit. Standard RADIUS mechanisms only allow fragmenting authentication data through multi-stage exchanges, not authorization data.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS peers exchange a series of smaller packets called chunks, each containing part of the large data. A new Frag-Status attribute signals when fragmentation is ongoing, and a State attribute ties chunks together. The process works before authentication (pre-authorization) when the client sends large data to the server, and after authentication (post-authorization) when the server sends large data to the client.
tldr.outcome: This experimental specification allows servers and clients to exchange more than 4096 bytes of authorization data while remaining compatible with existing RADIUS proxies that do not implement the fragmentation feature. The fragmented data is reconstructed and processed as if it had been received in a single packet.

today: RFC 7499 is an Experimental RFC published in April 2015. It defines a mechanism for fragmenting RADIUS packets to allow exchange of large amounts of authorization data exceeding the 4096-byte limit. The specification remains experimental and is undergoing testing in ABFAB deployments and related projects to verify real-world usability and operational behavior before potential advancement to Standards Track.

sections.title: The Problem and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 2865 defines RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), a protocol for carrying authentication, authorization, and accounting information between a RADIUS Client and RADIUS Server. Each RADIUS packet has a maximum size of 4096 bytes, a limit intended to avoid UDP fragmentation. This size was considered adequate when RADIUS was designed, but modern use cases require exchanging large amounts of authorization data.

Emerging scenarios, particularly the ABFAB (Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond web) architecture, require sending Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) statements from the server to the client. These statements are frequently larger than 4096 bytes. In some deployments, the RADIUS Client also needs to send large amounts of authorization data to the Server. Unlike authentication data (where multi-stage EAP exchanges are defined), no mechanism existed for fragmenting large authorization data across multiple packets. This document provides that mechanism in a way that remains compatible with existing RADIUS infrastructure.
sections.eli5: RADIUS messages have a size limit because they were designed for small authentication data. But now people need to send big documents (like employee access lists) in one message. This RFC shows how to chop up big messages into small pieces that fit the limit.

sections.title: Fragmentation Architecture and Scope
sections.content:
This specification limits fragmentation to authorization data (not accounting or Change-of-Authorization packets), and allows at most about 100 kilobytes of fragmented data to be sent. The specification defines two phases for authorization exchange: pre-authorization (before the end user is authenticated, with the client sending data to the server) and post-authorization (after authentication, with the server sending data to the client).

The mechanism is designed to be transparent to existing RADIUS proxies. Proxies that do not implement fragmentation can simply forward the packets without understanding the fragmentation process. The design carefully uses service type indicators that cause older RADIUS clients not implementing fragmentation to treat fragmented packets as if authentication had failed, making the mechanism fail-safe for legacy systems. The specification also does not require modification of intermediary proxies; only the endpoints that generate or consume fragmented data need to implement it.
sections.eli5: The system is designed to be invisible to old routers that pass messages between client and server. Old clients that don't understand fragmentation will just say 'I do not recognize this' and move on, rather than breaking.

sections.title: The Chunking Mechanism
sections.content:
When a RADIUS endpoint needs to send data exceeding the practical size limit (the minimum of 4096 bytes or the current Path MTU), the data is split into multiple smaller packets called chunks. Each chunk is a valid RADIUS packet containing a portion of the original attributes. The chunks are reassembled at the destination by simply concatenating them together.

Unlike IPv4 fragmentation, there is no Fragment Offset field; the chunks are explicitly ordered because RADIUS is a lock-step protocol. Chunk N+1 cannot be sent until all chunks up to and including N have been received and acknowledged. The ordering is enforced through the Frag-Status attribute, which signals whether fragmentation is ongoing (More-Data-Pending) or finished. A State attribute ties related chunks together by being copied from the previous response packet into the next request.

When a Long Extended Type attribute (as defined in RFC 6929) is split across chunks, a new T (Truncation) flag is set to indicate that the attribute continues in the next chunk. This is the only case where the chunking process modifies attribute content; the actual attribute values remain unchanged.
sections.eli5: Break the big message into pieces (chunks). Number them in order. Send one piece, wait for acknowledgment, send the next. The receiver sticks them back together in order. If a piece spans two chunks, mark it as 'continues next.'

sections.title: Pre-Authorization and Post-Authorization Exchange
sections.content:
Pre-authorization happens when the RADIUS Client sends large authorization data to the Server before the user is authenticated. The client sends the first chunk with a Frag-Status attribute set to More-Data-Pending. The server responds with an Access-Accept packet containing a State attribute and Frag-Status set to More-Data-Request. The client then sends the next chunk using the State from the previous response. This continues until the client sends a final chunk without a Frag-Status attribute. The server then processes all received attributes as if they had arrived in a single packet.

Post-authorization happens when the Server sends large authorization data to the Client after authentication is complete. The server sends the first chunk with Frag-Status = More-Data-Pending. The client responds with an Access-Request containing the State from that packet and Frag-Status = Fragmentation-Supported. The server continues sending chunks until it sends a final chunk without Frag-Status. The client then reconstructs and processes the received authorization data.

Each chunk MUST include certain attributes: User-Name (for proxy routing), Message-Authenticator (for security), and Service-Type = Additional-Authorization (to signal to older systems that this is a fragmented exchange, not a normal authorization). State is copied from the previous response to tie chunks together. This design ensures even transparent proxies that simply forward packets can pass fragments without modification.
sections.eli5: The conversation goes: 'I have a big message, part 1.' 'Got it, send part 2.' 'Here is part 2, one more coming.' 'Got it, send part 3.' 'Here is part 3, that is all.' 'Got it, processing the full message now.'

sections.title: Compatibility and Proxy Handling
sections.content:
This specification is designed to work with existing RADIUS proxies that do not implement fragmentation. A legacy proxy simply passes chunks forward because each chunk is a valid RADIUS packet. The User-Name attribute in each chunk allows proxies to route packets correctly based on user identity. The Frag-Status and Service-Type = Additional-Authorization attributes cause non-compliant RADIUS servers to return Access-Reject, allowing the client to detect incompatibility.

The specification requires two minor updates to standards-track documents. First, it allocates a new T (Truncation) flag in the Reserved field of the Long Extended Type attribute defined in RFC 6929, allowing attributes to be marked as continuing in the next chunk. Second, it notes that RFC 6158's statement 'attribute designers SHOULD NOT assume that a RADIUS implementation can successfully process RADIUS packets larger than 4096 bytes' is no longer universally true if this specification is widely implemented.

For systems not implementing fragmentation, the mechanism fails safely: older RADIUS clients see Service-Type with an unknown value and treat it as Access-Reject. Older RADIUS servers also receive packets with Service-Type = Additional-Authorization (an unknown service type) and respond with Access-Reject. Only endpoints implementing this specification recognize and handle fragmented exchanges correctly.
sections.eli5: Old systems that don't know about fragmentation just ignore the special attributes and say no. New systems that understand fragmentation use the special attributes to know which pieces go together. Everything still works because each piece is a valid message by itself.

sections.title: Security and Practical Limits
sections.content:
Each chunk is authenticated and validated independently. RADIUS security mechanisms (such as Message-Authenticator) are applied to each chunk separately. The Message-Authenticator attribute is calculated over each individual chunk, not over the reconstructed full packet. Neither integrity checks nor security checks are performed on the original (assembled) packet; each piece must be valid on its own.

The specification recommends that implementers limit fragmented data transfers to a maximum of 100 kilobytes. RADIUS/UDP transport is fundamentally unsuitable for bulk data transfer, as it lacks the retransmission policies and congestion control mechanisms of TCP. Larger data transfers should use RADIUS/TCP or other appropriate transport protocols instead. Administrators should adjust limitations based on the specific capabilities of their systems in terms of memory and processing power.

This is an Experimental RFC designed to test whether the fragmentation approach works in real-world deployments through ABFAB and related projects. The specification may advance to Standards Track if operational experience shows it is usable in large-scale environments.
sections.eli5: Each chunk is signed and checked. Do not send more than 100 kilobytes in chunks (use a better protocol if you need more). This is experimental; we are testing if it works in the real world.
